description: The gurdwara: its design, the palki and takht, its community role, and prayer in the home (GGS 305:4).
content_html:
What is a Gurdwara?

The word gurdwara means “doorway to the Guru” (from Punjabi: gur = Guru, dwara = door or gateway). Every gurdwara is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib — the eternal, living scripture that Sikhs regard as their eleventh and final Guru. Without the Guru Granth Sahib, a building is not a gurdwara. This understanding shapes everything about how the gurdwara is designed and used.

There are over 250 registered gurdwaras in the United Kingdom, serving the approximately 430,000 Sikhs in Britain. The largest is the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, west London — the largest gurdwara outside India — which can accommodate over 3,000 worshippers and serves langar to thousands of people each week. Gurdwaras in cities including Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and Glasgow are centres of spiritual, cultural and social life for their local Sikh communities.

Design and Features

From the outside, a gurdwara is identifiable by the Nishan Sahib — a tall flagpole flying a triangular dark blue flag bearing the Khanda (the Sikh emblem). Inside, the main prayer hall is called the Darbar Sahib (literally “court of the Lord”). Worshippers remove their shoes and cover their heads before entering as a mark of respect. They then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and make an offering.

The prayer hall has no fixed seating or pews. The congregation sits on the floor — regardless of age, gender or status — which itself expresses the Sikh belief in equality. There is no distinction between where men and women sit in the prayer hall of a gurdwara; they may sit on either side or intermixed, depending on local practice, but the principle is complete equality.

Key Fact

The two most important features in the gurdwara prayer hall are the palki (throne-canopy) and the takht (throne or royal seat). Together they represent the sovereignty and living authority of the Guru Granth Sahib.

The Palki and the Takht

The palki is the ornate canopy or palanquin structure under which the Guru Granth Sahib rests. It is typically elaborately decorated and elevated, signalling the supreme honour in which the scripture is held. The palki symbolises the royal status of the Guru Granth Sahib — just as an earthly king might sit under a canopy, the eternal Guru sits under its palki.

The takht (throne) is the raised platform or seat on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed. The word takht literally means “throne.” Together, the palki (canopy) and the takht (throne) communicate that the Guru Granth Sahib is not just a book — it is the living, reigning Guru of the Sikh community, deserving of the same honour as a Guru in human form. Beside the takht stands the chauri — a fan waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a mark of honour, similar to the fans once used to cool royalty.

The Guru Granth Sahib is treated with the same care as a living person. At the end of each day in many gurdwaras, the scripture is ceremonially “put to rest” in a dedicated room called the sukhasan room, wrapped in cloth (rumala). In the morning, it is ceremonially brought back to the prayer hall in a procession. This practice underlines the Sikh belief that the Guru Granth Sahib is not a sacred object but a living presence — the Guru who is always available to the community.

The Gurdwara’s Role in the Community

The gurdwara is far more than a place of formal worship. It is the social, cultural and spiritual heart of the Sikh community. The original vision of Guru Nanak was that the gurdwara should serve three interconnected purposes, sometimes described as the three pillars of Sikhism: Naam Japna (meditation on God’s name), Kirat Karni (honest work) and Vand Chakna (sharing with others). All three are expressed in and through the gurdwara.

The gurdwara hosts the langar (free communal kitchen), classes in Punjabi, Sikh history and scripture, ceremonies for birth, naming, marriage and death, and welfare services for those in need. In many British cities, gurdwaras have opened food banks, offered shelter to homeless people, and provided community support during times of national crisis — including during the COVID-19 pandemic. This is sewa in action.

Sikh practice is not confined to the gurdwara. The Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 305:4 emphasises the importance of prayer and remembrance of God in the home. Amritdhari Sikhs observe the Nitnem — a set of daily prayers including Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak) in the morning, and further prayers in the evening and at night. Many Sikh families maintain a dedicated space in the home for the Guru Granth Sahib or for a prayer area. The home is understood as an extension of the gurdwara in spiritual terms — the family that prays together strengthens the sangat in miniature.

Sahajdhari Sikhs — those who follow Sikh teachings but have not undergone formal initiation — may practise Nitnem and maintain home prayer spaces without being bound by all the obligations of the Khalsa. The principle of prayer in the home (GGS 305:4) applies to all Sikhs, amritdhari and sahajdhari alike.

Key Fact

The gurdwara serves the whole community, not just practising Sikhs. It hosts the langar (free communal meal), welfare services, education and ceremonies — expressing the Sikh teaching that sewa (service) is not optional but a dimension of worship. In Britain, gurdwaras have been at the forefront of community support in times of hardship.
exam_tip_html:
When answering a question about the gurdwara, make sure you distinguish the palki (the ornate canopy over the Guru Granth Sahib) from the takht (the throne or seat on which it rests). Students frequently confuse these two terms. The key point for the exam is that both express the same belief: the Guru Granth Sahib is not merely a book but the living, reigning Guru deserving of royal honour.

For the 6-mark Explain question on the role of the gurdwara, cite GGS 305:4 as your named source of authority for the importance of prayer in the home. This is a specific Sikh source reference that immediately shows awareness of the scripture. Then develop two reasons: the gurdwara as a place of worship, and the gurdwara as a centre for sewa and community. Each reason needs to be developed with “because” or “this means that” reasoning.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The gurdwara (‘doorway to the Guru’) is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Key features include the palki (ornate canopy) and the takht (throne) — both expressing the Guru Granth Sahib’s status as the living, reigning Guru.
  • The gurdwara is the social, cultural and spiritual heart of the Sikh community, hosting worship, langar, education, ceremonies and welfare services — all expressions of sewa.
  • Prayer in the home is also important (GGS 305:4) — amritdhari Sikhs observe Nitnem (daily prayers) and many Sikh families maintain a dedicated prayer space, making the home an extension of the gurdwara’s spiritual purpose.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the 'palki' in a gurdwara?
A) The raised platform where worshippers sit
B) The ornate canopy over the throne of the Guru Granth Sahib
C) The flag flown outside the gurdwara
D) The room where the Guru Granth Sahib rests at night
practice_questions.marks: B) The ornate canopy over the throne of the Guru Granth Sahib [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Sikh flag flown outside every gurdwara.
State two roles of the gurdwara in the Sikh community beyond formal worship.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: hosting the langar (free communal meal); providing education in Punjabi, scripture and Sikh history; hosting birth, naming, marriage and death ceremonies; providing welfare and community support services.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which features of the gurdwara express Sikh beliefs.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- The palki and takht: the ornate canopy and throne housing the Guru Granth Sahib express the belief that the scripture is the living, reigning Guru — deserving of the same honour as a Guru in human form (1 + 1 marks).
- The congregation sitting on the floor: because all sit on the floor regardless of status or gender, the layout expresses the Sikh belief in the equality of all people before God (1 + 1 marks).
- The Nishan Sahib: the flag outside signals the gurdwara as a place of welcome for all, reflecting the Sikh teaching that all people are equal in God's sight and welcome to enter (1 + 1 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the gurdwara is important to Sikhs.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two developed reasons with reference to the Guru Granth Sahib (e.g. GGS 305:4 on prayer) or Sikh teaching. Possible points: (1) The gurdwara is where the Guru Granth Sahib is housed — because the scripture is regarded as the living Guru, being in its presence is being in the presence of God's word; this makes the gurdwara the centre of Sikh spiritual life. (2) The gurdwara enacts sewa through langar and community services — the GGS teaches that serving others is serving God; the gurdwara's open-door policy and free meals make this teaching concrete for the whole community.
Secure (3-4 marks): Reasons present, mostly accurate; source named but underdeveloped.
Developing (1-2 marks): One reason, limited development, source absent.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
'The gurdwara is the most important element of Sikh practice.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
- refer to Sikh teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The gurdwara is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib — the living Guru — making it the spiritual centre of Sikh life. All major practices (akhand path, langar, nam japna, kirtan) take place in or through the gurdwara.
- The gurdwara expresses all three pillars of Sikhism (Naam Japna, Kirat Karni, Vand Chakna) simultaneously — it is the community structure that holds Sikh practice together.
- For Sikhs in Britain, especially recent migrants, the gurdwara has been an essential social anchor — providing community, language support, welfare, and cultural continuity in a new country.

Arguments against:
- Prayer in the home (GGS 305:4) is equally important — Guru Nanak taught that God is not confined to a building; sincere prayer and nam simran at home are fully valid expressions of Sikh devotion.
- Amritdhari Sikhs observe Nitnem (daily prayers) and sewa regardless of whether they attend a gurdwara — the inner commitment to God is primary.
- Sahajdhari Sikhs may rarely attend the gurdwara yet be deeply sincere in their faith — suggesting practice is not defined by building attendance alone.
- The Guru Granth Sahib itself teaches that God is found within the heart, not in any external location.

Mastering (10-12 marks): Both sides argued with Sikh sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, some sources, conclusion.
Developing (4-6 marks): Mostly one-sided, limited sources.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.
